compensating.why: hop 2 keeps the marker bit in the value of the first byte
hop 3 masks the value of the first byte to seven bits
hop 4 reads at most eight bytes of the number

ownership_reason: Only the gold reads the bytes that follow the first byte of a binary field and folds them into the value; hop 1 reads only the marker bit, hop 2 only the first byte (its low seven bits become the leading value), hops 3 and 4 pass the buffer along, and all four get back one long. A Java byte cannot hold 0x80 or more as a positive number, so no caller can prepare the buffer so that an unmasked addition of the bytes comes out right, and the gold's result is the only place the bytes are combined. The convention that each byte of a binary number is an unsigned 8-bit value is pinned outside the gold: CpioUtil.byteArray2long does the same big-endian fold with every byte masked (ret <<= 8; ret |= b & 0xFF; CpioUtilTest oldBinMagicFromByteArrayNotSwapped, byte 0xc7 after the first, passes); ZipLong.getValue masks every byte (ZipLongTest testSign: ff ff ff ff is 0xFFFFFFFF); TarUtils.parseName masks each byte to allow for sign extension (TarUtilsTest testRoundTripNames, bytes 0xb1); TarUtils.formatLongOctalOrBinaryBytes writes the binary form as the 8-bit bytes of the value with the marker bit set, and TarArchiveOutputStreamTest testBigFileStarMode reads such a field back through the chain. The facade's javadoc says the rest of the buffer is interpreted as a binary number, and the gold's javadoc promises the value of that binary number, which for ff ff ff ff ff ff ff ff with the marker bit dropped is 0x7fffffffffffffff.
